presentingComplaint: Progressive abdominal distension, leg swelling and drowsiness over 2 weeks
history: Known alcohol-related cirrhosis (Child-Pugh B at last clinic, ongoing intermittent alcohol use until 3 weeks ago). Background type 2 diabetes for 15 years with diabetic nephropathy and stage 3b chronic kidney disease (baseline creatinine ~1.8 mg/dL, on file). Over the past fortnight he has developed increasing abdominal girth, bilateral pedal oedema, reduced urine output and, in the last 3 days, day-night reversal, poor concentration and one episode of confusion noted by his wife. Reports mild reduction in appetite but no haematemesis, melena, fever or abdominal pain. Regular medications: spironolactone, furosemide, propranolol, metformin (self-reduced), gliclazide, and recent over-the-counter NSAIDs for knee pain. No recent hospitalisation. The coexisting CKD and diabetes confound the volume and renal picture, raising the question of whether the deterioration is cardiorenal, diabetic nephropathy progression or hepatic decompensation.
examination: Deeply icteric, cachectic with temporal wasting. Multiple spider naevi over chest, palmar erythema, gynaecomastia. Abdomen grossly distended with tense ascites, shifting dullness and everted umbilicus; non-tender, no guarding, mild splenomegaly, liver not enlarged. Bilateral pitting pedal oedema to the knees. Asterixis clearly demonstrable with outstretched hands; drowsy but rousable and oriented to person only (grade 2 encephalopathy). No focal neurological deficit, no neck stiffness. Chest clear, JVP not raised. No stigmata of active GI bleeding on PR.
imaging: Abdominal ultrasound with Doppler: shrunken, coarse, nodular liver with surface irregularity consistent with cirrhosis; gross ascites; splenomegaly (14.5 cm); patent but reduced portal vein flow with recanalised umbilical vein. Kidneys show bilateral increased echogenicity with reduced cortical thickness consistent with chronic parenchymal disease, no hydronephrosis. No portal vein thrombosis.
microbiology: Diagnostic ascitic tap: straw-coloured fluid, PMN count 90 cells/mm3 (below 250 threshold), Gram stain negative, culture pending/no growth — no evidence of spontaneous bacterial peritonitis. Blood cultures negative.
differentialDiagnoses: Decompensated cirrhosis (ascites + hepatic encephalopathy) precipitated by NSAID use and diuretic overuse
Hepatorenal syndrome / hepatic encephalopathy as isolated decompensation
Progression of diabetic CKD with fluid overload
Occult variceal / GI bleed as encephalopathy precipitant
finalDiagnosis: Decompensated cirrhosis with new-onset grade 2 ascites and grade 2 hepatic encephalopathy, complicated by acute kidney injury on chronic kidney disease (NSAID- and diuretic-precipitated), on a background of alcohol-related cirrhosis and diabetic nephropathy
citations: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22e — Cirrhosis and Its Complications
EASL Clinical Practice Guidelines — Decompensated Cirrhosis, 2018
AASLD Practice Guidance — Ascites and Hepatorenal Syndrome, 2021
stewardship: Non-infective decompensation: no empiric antibiotics indicated as ascitic PMN <250/mm3, blood and ascitic cultures negative, and no clinical sepsis. Management is source-directed at precipitants — stop NSAIDs, hold/reduce diuretics, treat encephalopathy with lactulose (and rifaximin as gut-directed therapy, not systemic antimicrobial stewardship), cautious volume assessment given CKD. Reserve antibiotics only if SBP or other infection is subsequently confirmed.
contraindications: Avoid nephrotoxins (NSAIDs, aminoglycosides, iodinated contrast) given AKI-on-CKD
Avoid aggressive diuresis / large-volume paracentesis without albumin cover given renal impairment
Avoid benzodiazepines and sedatives which worsen hepatic encephalopathy
Cautious metformin use / hold in renal impairment and acute illness (lactic acidosis risk)
edgeCases: Coexisting CKD raises baseline creatinine, masking the true severity of AKI and confounding hepatorenal syndrome diagnosis
Diuretic-driven hyponatraemia and hyperkalaemia can independently precipitate encephalopathy
Diabetic nephropathy fluid overload can mimic worsening ascites/oedema
A normal PMN count does not exclude a resolving or early infection; repeat tap if deteriorates
expectedMaiK: Recognise multi-system decompensated cirrhosis (ascites + encephalopathy + AKI-on-CKD) and identify NSAID/diuretic precipitants rather than mislabelling as primary renal or cardiac failure.
